clue.text: Matter of a recent tercentenary

parts.note: Charles I was beheaded in 1649, so a puzzle of 1949 could call that execution the subject of a recent three-hundredth anniversary

explanation.surface: A solemn note about some anniversary being marked three centuries on.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives no hint of which event; the puzzle dates from around 1949, three hundred years after Charles I lost his head in Whitehall.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles I's execution in 1649 was a beheading, an event whose 300th anniversary fell in 1949.

annotationWithheld.clue: A portion of fish in Salford

clue.text: I pray thee, Rosalind, sweet my be merry (As You Like It)

definitions.text: I pray thee, Rosalind, sweet my be merry (As You Like It)

parts.words: I pray thee, Rosalind, sweet my be merry (As You Like It)
parts.note: Celia's opening words to Rosalind in Act 1 of the play, with the word of endearment left out for the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare quoted with a gap where one word should be.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Celia says 'I pray thee, Rosalind, sweet my coz, be merry'. The missing word is Elizabethan shorthand for cousin.
explanation.definitionFit: Celia and Rosalind are cousins, and Shakespeare's Celia calls her by the clipped form of 'cousin'.

clue.text: Rabelaisian rogue suggests more than a flash in it

parts.note: in the phrase 'a flash in the pan' the thing the flash is in is the pan
an urge is a lasting impulse, more than a momentary flash of feeling

explanation.surface: Someone suggests the rascal from Rabelais is more than a passing flash.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the idiom 'a flash in the pan': 'in it' points at the pan, and something more than a passing flash is a sustained urge.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel features a cunning, roguish companion of Pantagruel by this name.

clue.text: Stock-in-trade of the town-crier?

parts.note: reads 'town-crier' as someone who makes a whole town weep rather than a bellman making announcements

explanation.surface: A question about what a town crier with his bell keeps in stock.
explanation.walkthrough: A town crier was the official who shouted public announcements; here the phrase is taken as one who makes the town cry, and the means is a lachrymatory gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Riot police use this irritant gas because it makes people's eyes stream, as if crying.

clue.text: One is better for using it

definitions.text: One is better for using it

parts.words: One is better for using it
parts.note: 'better' is read as 'bettor', one who places bets, rather than as 'improved'

explanation.surface: A claim that some practice improves whoever uses it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' sounds like self-improvement, but it is the gambler: a person who bets through the machine that pools stakes and works out the odds.
explanation.definitionFit: A tote machine pools wagers at a racecourse and calculates the payouts, so it is a punter's tool.

clue.text: Make fast to nothing

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Make fast to nothing': O (nothing) + LENT (fast) builds the letters, but 'Make' cannot define a word meaning smelling or odorous; the defining word appears to be misread and no scan or reprint is available

clue.text: Where do we go from here ?" North inevitably

definitions.text: Where do we go from here ?" North inevitably

parts.words: Where do we go from here ?" North inevitably
parts.note: a spot from which every direction you can travel is northward, so the only answer to the question is north

explanation.surface: A traveller asks where to head next and gets the reply that it must be north.
explanation.walkthrough: The question sounds like everyday indecision; the reply 'North inevitably' is literally true only at one point on Earth, the southern end of its axis.
explanation.definitionFit: At the southernmost point of the globe every compass bearing leads northward.

clue.text: Lost in fiction

parts.note: the word 'Lost' begins the title of a famous novel, and the solver supplies the word that follows it

explanation.surface: Someone who has gone missing inside a story.
explanation.walkthrough: James Hilton's 1933 novel Lost Horizon, which introduced Shangri-La, completes the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilton's novel title pairs 'Lost' with this word for the line where earth meets sky.

clue.text: She doesn't want anyone to take her part

definitions.text: She doesn't want anyone to take her part

parts.words: She doesn't want anyone to take her part
parts.note: 'take her part' is read as taking over her stage role rather than siding with her

explanation.surface: A woman who wants no one to stand up for her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take her part' usually means to support someone; here it means stepping into her role, which an understudy might do.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who plays a role on stage or screen guards her part against rivals.

clue.text: Oliver Cromwell's college

parts.note: a plain description of where the Lord Protector studied at Cambridge

explanation.surface: A note about the college Oliver Cromwell attended.
explanation.walkthrough: Cromwell entered this Cambridge college in 1616, and his head is buried in its chapel.
explanation.definitionFit: Cromwell was a student at this Cambridge foundation, so it was his college.

clue.text: Trickster of note

explanation.surface: A con man who is well known.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of note' suggests fame, but it means a musical note raised a semitone.
explanation.definitionFit: A card cheat is called by this word, and a note raised by a semitone carries the same name.

clue.text: Writers should enclose a stamped addressed envelope when they do

definitions.text: Writers should enclose a stamped addressed envelope when they do

parts.words: Writers should enclose a stamped addressed envelope when they do
parts.note: read as advice to authors who send manuscripts by mail, which split into the two words post and scripts

explanation.surface: Etiquette advice that writers send a return envelope with their submissions.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as POST SCRIPTS: authors mailing manuscripts should include return postage. Whole, it is the afterthoughts added below a letter's signature.
explanation.definitionFit: Added notes after a signature are what writers append, and posting their manuscripts is what authors do.

clue.text: Great duel, presumably well organized

indicators.note: says the words great duel are only presumably what they seem, so their letters are to be taken in another order

explanation.surface: A big formal duel would presumably be run under strict rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presumably' signals the anagram of GREAT DUEL; the surface also works because a formal duel was run by rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Something controlled by rules is orderly, well run and properly ordered.

clue.text: Faun's nest. (anag.)

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Faun's nest. (anag.)': an anagram of FAUNS NEST with no definition at all, so no definition can be marked

clue.text: A dance of the moment, probably 11

explanation.surface: A dance in fashion now, likely a keen one.
explanation.walkthrough: Khachaturian's Sabre Dance was a hit tune of the late 1940s. Entry 11 is the word for keen-edged, as a cavalry blade would be.
explanation.definitionFit: Khachaturian's Sabre Dance was a popular piece then, and a cavalry sword is keen-edged, the meaning of entry 11.

clue.text: Worn by Sally and Sampson?

parts.note: Sally suggests the Salvation Army, whose bands play brass, and Sampson suggests a high-ranking officer, both pointing at headgear

explanation.surface: A question about what two people called Sally and Sampson wear.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Sally Army' is a British nickname for the Salvation Army, famous for its brass bands; Admiral Sampson suggests the gold-braided caps of senior officers, nicknamed brass hats.
explanation.definitionFit: Senior military officers are called brass hats after the gold braid on their caps.

clue.text: County threatened by legislation

explanation.surface: A shire whose existence is put at risk by a new law.
explanation.walkthrough: Huntingdonshire, a former English county, is abbreviated this way; fox hunting faced anti-hunting bills.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation for Huntingdonshire, a former English county, is also the name for chases with hounds, which bans have targeted.

clue.text: Dogged Frenchmen

parts.note: 'Dogged' suggests stubborn, but it points to a breed of dog, and the Frenchmen are people of a region in France

explanation.surface: A description of stubborn Frenchmen.
explanation.walkthrough: The breed Britons called the Alsatian is the German Shepherd; the people of Alsace in eastern France share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The natives of Alsace in France share their name with the dog breed elsewhere called German Shepherd.

clue.text: Cordial I see and embrace it

indicators.note: the word 'and' wraps itself around the letters of 'I see', which it holds like an embrace

explanation.surface: A friendly greeting: I see you and give you a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Embrace it' means 'and' encloses the 'it' just mentioned, I SEE, giving AN-ISEE-D. 'Cordial' looks like an adjective but is the liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: A liqueur flavoured with this seed is a cordial, an old word for a sweet alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Is? Perhaps it accounts for being cut!

definitions.text: Is? Perhaps it accounts for being cut!

parts.words: Is? Perhaps it accounts for being cut!
parts.note: the little word 'is' is pictured as a longer word such as 'this' or 'his' that has been clipped of its first letters

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about why something has been cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: The word IS may be THIS or HIS with the front cut off, like hair or wool trimmed away.
explanation.definitionFit: Wool clipped from a sheep or hair cut short has been trimmed, as a word losing letters is.

clue.text: Where the trumpets sounded for Mr. Valiant-for-Truth

definitions.text: Where the trumpets sounded for Mr. Valiant-for-Truth

parts.words: Where the trumpets sounded for Mr. Valiant-for-Truth
parts.note: Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress ends Valiant-for-Truth's story with 'all the trumpets sounded for him on the ...'

explanation.surface: A question about where a pilgrim was welcomed with fanfares.
explanation.walkthrough: A quotation from Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress: as Mr Valiant-for-Truth crosses the river of death, the trumpets sound for him beyond it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Bunyan the far bank of the river of death is heaven, where the trumpets greet the pilgrim.

clue.text: Had she put on weight it wouldn't have been avoirdupois

definitions.text: Had she put on weight it wouldn't have been avoirdupois

parts.words: Had she put on weight it wouldn't have been avoirdupois
parts.note: points to the woman of Troy, since troy weight is the system that is not avoirdupois

explanation.surface: A remark about which weighing system would apply if a woman got heavier.
explanation.walkthrough: Avoirdupois and troy are two systems of weights; a famous woman of Troy would gain troy weight.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous beauty of Troy carries the city's name, and troy is the other scale of weights.

clue.text: All-the-way flowers

parts.note: the idiom '... all the way' means unbroken success, so the flowers that go all the way are these blooms

explanation.surface: Flowers that line an entire route.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'roses all the way' describes something pleasant from start to finish.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for an easy, pleasant course names these fragrant garden blooms.

clue.text: A dark horse, but famous

parts.note: an unknown runner is a dark horse; here the famous horse is one whose name means a darkening of the sun

explanation.surface: An unexpected contender who is nonetheless well known.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'dark horse' is normally an unknown contender; here it is a celebrated racehorse of the 1760s whose name is the sun's darkening.
explanation.definitionFit: The great 18th-century racehorse bore the name of the darkening when the moon hides the sun.

clue.text: Characteristic of the people of Flushing?

definitions.text: Characteristic of the people of Flushing?

parts.words: Characteristic of the people of Flushing?
parts.note: Flushing is a Dutch port, but read as a verb it means blushing, which shows on the cheeks

explanation.surface: A question about what marks out the inhabitants of a Dutch port.
explanation.walkthrough: Flushing is the English name of Vlissingen in the Netherlands; read as 'people who are flushing' it means those who are blushing.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who are blushing show a reddened complexion from embarrassment.

clue.text: Penniless dandy in debt

indicators.note: without a penny, so the letter for an old penny is dropped from the word for a dandy

parts.note: a dude is a dandified man of fashion

explanation.surface: A dandy who has no money and owes it to others.
explanation.walkthrough: D was the symbol for the old British penny (from Latin denarius); 'Penniless' removes it from DUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Money that is owing and unpaid is outstanding, as one in debt has payments outstanding.

clue.text: Exhibited by people with no wish to make a match of it, perhaps

definitions.text: Exhibited by people with no wish to make a match of it, perhaps

parts.words: Exhibited by people with no wish to make a match of it, perhaps
parts.note: a match is a close contest; people who want no contest favour only their own view, or a game that is all one way

explanation.surface: Something shown by people who don't want an even contest.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'make a match of it' is to make a contest close; those who refuse show bias toward one party.
explanation.definitionFit: Bias toward one party or view, the opposite of fairness, is the quality meant.
